questions.prompt: How did Metchnikoff first observe phagocytosis?

options.text: He grew white blood cells on agar plates
He stained human blood with crystal violet
He filtered bacteria from broth and injected guinea pigs
He poked bacteria into transparent starfish larvae and watched cells eat them

questions.explanation: Starfish larvae are see-through, so he could watch phagocytes engulf the bacteria.

questions.prompt: A fever attacks any microbe and is no stronger the tenth time you get sick. Fever is therefore part of:
questions.explanation: Innate defenses are inborn, target no specific antigen, and don't improve.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the lines of defense is FALSE?

options.text: Inflammation is part of the third line of defense.
Phagocytosis is part of the second line of defense.
Intact skin is part of the first line of defense.
Memory is a feature of the third line of defense.
Antibody-mediated immunity is part of the third line.

questions.prompt: Which feature does NOT help skin resist microbes?
questions.explanation: Skin is dry — low moisture limits bacterial growth.

questions.prompt: A heavy smoker has a constant 'smoker's cough.' Which defense has been damaged?
questions.explanation: Without beating cilia, coughing is the only way to move mucus up the airway.

questions.prompt: Lysozyme in tears, saliva, sweat, and urine kills bacteria by:
questions.explanation: It mainly attacks Gram-positive cell walls.

questions.prompt: Which body fluid has the lowest pH, about 2?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach destroys most swallowed microbes.

questions.prompt: Trace what happens to mucus and trapped bacteria from the trachea to the point where they are destroyed.
questions.explanation: Goblet cells secrete sticky mucus that traps inhaled bacteria; the ciliary escalator moves the mucus (1–3 cm/hr) up the trachea to the throat; it is swallowed and the bacteria are destroyed by stomach acid (pH ~2).

questions.prompt: What triggers the inflammatory response after a cut?
questions.explanation: Histamine is the key chemical trigger.

questions.prompt: Why does an inflamed area become red and warm?

options.text: Histamine dilates vessels, bringing more warm blood
Bacteria in the tissue produce heat as they grow
Pus is red and hot, so it colors the skin
Vessels constrict and trap blood under the skin

questions.prompt: Why does an inflamed area swell?

options.text: Dilated vessels become leaky and fluid collects
Mast cells swell up after releasing histamine
Macrophages release gas as they digest bacteria
Bacteria multiply into a lump under the skin

questions.explanation: The swelling also causes the pain.

questions.prompt: Which statement about phagocytes is FALSE?

options.text: Macrophages die from overeating, just like neutrophils.

questions.explanation: Macrophages survive because they digest and excrete the waste; neutrophils eat themselves to death.

questions.prompt: In phagocytosis, what forms when a lysosome fuses with a phagosome?
questions.explanation: Hydrolytic enzymes then digest the microbe.

questions.prompt: Toll-like receptors on macrophages recognize which kind of molecules?

options.text: Common foreign molecules like mannose and LPS
The patient's own proteins on healthy cells
Only one specific antigen per macrophage
Histamine released by nearby mast cells

questions.explanation: They recognize broad features shared by many microbes, so phagocytosis stays nonspecific.

options.text: Histamine, sebum, and dead skin cells
Dead neutrophils, phagocytic waste, and fluid
Live bacteria and nothing else at all
Red blood cells and platelets only

questions.prompt: Name the four signs and symptoms of inflammation and explain the cause of each.
questions.explanation: Redness and heat come from histamine-driven vasodilation bringing more blood; swelling comes from leaky dilated vessels letting fluid into tissue; pain comes from the swelling.
